title: Testing yourself: retrieval practice
keyIdea: Retrieval practice means pulling what you learned out of your memory, with the notes shut, and then checking. Each time you recall a fact, it gets easier to recall next time. Good ways to do it are question flashcards, a brain dump of everything you remember, and practice questions. Always check your answers and fix the gaps. Cards you miss come back soon, and cards you get right come back later.

kid: Most people revise by reading their notes again. It feels like it works. But reading only puts facts in. A test asks you to get them out. Getting facts out is a skill, and you get better at it by doing it.

So test yourself. Shut the book, then try to answer. Use flashcards with a question on the front and the answer on the back. Or write down all you can remember about a topic. That is called a brain dump.
Then check. Open your notes and mark what you got right. Fix what was wrong. Add what you missed. The gaps you find show you what to practise next. If you never check, a wrong answer can stick.
Try hard before you flip a card. It is fine to get it wrong. The effort of trying is what helps. Put cards you miss in a pile for tomorrow. Cards you get right still come back, just a few days later.
adult: Retrieval practice has some of the strongest evidence of any study method. A big 2013 review by Dunlosky and others looked at ten methods. Practice testing was one of only two rated highly useful. Rereading and highlighting were rated low. The gain holds across ages, subjects and kinds of test.

Why it works: each time you recall something, the route back to that memory gets stronger. Next time, it comes back faster and more surely. A little struggle helps, as long as you check after. In one well-known study, students who recalled a text did better a week later than students who read it again. Yet they felt less sure of themselves.

Common mistakes: cards that give the answer away or copy whole notes, and flipping a card before really trying. Others skip the check, so errors are never fixed. Some drop cards once they are right, or only practise the easy ones. Another trap is to treat a low score as a verdict on you. It is really a map of what to study next.

In the lab you judge five flashcard fronts. You read some notes, cover them and answer four cards. You file Sam's checked cards into Leitner boxes, and mark a brain dump against the notes to fill its gaps. Last, you plan thirty minutes of revision and watch how test-ready you get.

familyTip: Before a test, swap roles: your child makes five question cards and quizzes you, then you quiz them. Keep the book shut until each answer has been tried, then check together. Put any missed cards on top of the pile for tomorrow.

visual.caption: Good flashcard front or needs fixing? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: What is the capital of Spain?
Madrid is the capital of Spain.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: judge flashcard fronts, recall with notes covered, file cards in Leitner boxes, check a brain dump and plan revision.

practice.prompt: Which is the best way to get ready for a spelling test?
choices: Cover the words and write them from memory
Read the list over and over
practice.hint: Which one makes you pull the spellings out of your memory?
practice.explain: Writing them from memory is a test. Each try makes the spellings easier to recall, and checking shows which ones need more work.

practice.prompt: Ava has {n} flashcards in Box 1 after her quiz. What do these cards mean?
choices: She missed them, so she practises them soon
practice.hint: Box 1 is for cards that come back tomorrow. Which cards need that?
practice.explain: The {n} cards in Box 1 are the ones Ava missed or peeked at. They need practice soon, so she sees them again tomorrow.

practice.prompt: Which flashcard front is the most useful?
choices: What gas do plants take in?
practice.hint: A good front asks one clear question and does not give the answer.
practice.explain: A question makes you recall the answer. A front that states the fact gives it away, and one word is too vague to test.

practice.prompt: Leo wrote a brain dump with {n} ideas about volcanoes. What should he do next?
choices: Check it against his notes and fix the gaps
practice.hint: A brain dump is only half the job. What finds the mistakes?
practice.explain: Leo should mark his {n} ideas against his notes, fix anything wrong and add what he missed. Those gaps tell him what to practise.

choices: Pulling facts out of memory, then checking
pool.hint: Retrieve means to get something back. From where?
pool.explain: Retrieval practice means getting facts back out of your memory with the notes shut, then checking. That makes them easier to recall later.

pool.prompt: Mo got {n} cards right in his quiz. What should happen to those cards?
choices: Test them again in a few days
Test them again in one minute
pool.hint: Memories fade if you stop recalling them. When should right cards come back?
pool.explain: Right cards still come back, just later. Seeing those {n} cards again in a few days keeps them strong without wasting time.

pool.prompt: You are stuck on a flashcard. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Try hard to recall, then flip and check
pool.hint: The effort of trying is what helps. But you also need the right answer.
pool.explain: Trying first makes your memory work. Then flipping shows you if you were right, so a wrong answer does not stick.

pool.prompt: Why does testing yourself beat re-reading?
choices: Recalling a fact makes it easier to recall later
pool.hint: A test asks you to get facts out. Which method practises that?
pool.explain: Each time you recall a fact, the route back to it gets stronger. Re-reading only feels good because the words look familiar.

pool.prompt: Zara has {n} minutes to revise. Which plan is best?
choices: Test herself, check, then test again
Re-read her notes the whole time
Highlight her notes the whole time
pool.hint: Which plan makes her recall, find her gaps and then fix them?
pool.explain: In {n} minutes, testing, checking and testing again builds far more memory than re-reading or highlighting.

pool.prompt: A quiz shows you got 2 questions wrong. What does that tell you?
choices: That you are bad at the subject
pool.hint: Is a wrong answer a judgement or a clue?
pool.explain: Mistakes in a self-test are useful. They show exactly which bits to practise next, so you fix them before the real test.

pool.prompt: Which is the best flashcard front?
choices: How many legs does an insect have?
pool.hint: The front should ask one question you can answer from memory.
pool.explain: One clear question makes you recall the answer. The other fronts give the answer away or have far too much on them.
